name: Samarkand
info: Samarkand is a city in the Zarafshan valley of south-eastern Uzbekistan, one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities of Central Asia, a Sogdian city, a Silk Road centre and the capital of Timur.

facts.founded: The date of founding is uncertain; researchers at the Institute of Archaeology of Samarkand date it to around 700 BCE, and it has been proposed that the city was established in the 8th or 7th century BCE.
facts.where: In the valley of the Zarafshan river in south-eastern Uzbekistan, 270 km by road from Tashkent and 240 km from Bukhara.
facts.known: The Sogdian city of Marakanda; conquest by Alexander in 329 BCE; the legend of the first paper mill of the Islamic world; the Mongol sack of 1220; Timur’s capital; Ulugh Beg’s observatory; the Registan, the Gur-i Amir and Shah-i-Zinda
facts.today: Samarkand is the second-largest city of Uzbekistan and the capital of the Samarkand Region.

t: Samarkand was a central city of the Sogdian civilisation and was conquered in turn by Alexander in 329 BCE, the Sasanians, the Umayyads in about 712, the Mongols in 1220 and the Russians in 1868.
Timur made it his capital in 1370 and rebuilt most of it, and his grandson Ulugh Beg built a madrasa on the Registan and an observatory there in 1428.
Under the Uzbek khans, the Russian Empire and the Soviet Union the city kept its monuments, though some were destroyed, and Persian remained its literary language.
dyk: According to legend, the secret of papermaking was obtained from two Chinese prisoners taken at the Battle of Talas in 751, which led to the first paper mill in the Islamic world, at Samarkand.

sections.origins:
Samarkand stands in the valley of the Zarafshan river in south-eastern Uzbekistan. Excavations within the city and in its suburbs have unearthed evidence of human activity 40,000 years old, from the Upper Palaeolithic, and a group of Mesolithic sites lies in the suburbs. There is no direct evidence of when the city was founded. Researchers at the Institute of Archaeology of Samarkand date it to around 700 BCE, and it has been proposed that it was established between the 8th and 7th centuries BCE. The canals that brought water to the city and its suburbs, the Syob and the Darg’om, appeared around the 7th to 5th centuries BCE.

After the Indo-Iranian migrations of the second millennium BCE Samarkand became one of the main centres of the Sogdian civilisation, and under the Achaemenid dynasty of Persia it was the capital of the Sogdian satrapy. The Greeks called it Marakanda. Some sources derive the present name from the Sogdian samar (stone) and kand (fort or town), which cannot be proved; the 11th-century scholar Mahmud al-Kashghari gave the Karakhanid Turkic form Sämizkänd, “fat city”. Archaeologists have found remains of Nestorian buildings at the ancient site of Afrasiyab. In the early Middle Ages the city had four rows of defensive walls and four gates.
sections.growth:
Alexander took the city in 329 BCE. It suffered significant damage but recovered rapidly under Hellenic influence, which brought new construction techniques: square bricks replaced oblong ones, and better masonry and plastering appeared. It then passed to the Seleucid Empire, the Greco-Bactrian Kingdom and the Kushan Empire. When the Kushans lost Sogdia in the 3rd century CE Samarkand declined as a centre of power, and it did not revive significantly until the 5th century.

Under the Samanids (875 to 999) the city was a capital and a node of trade routes, and New Persian gradually replaced Sogdian as the main language of the region. From 1040 to 1212 it was the capital of the Western Qarakhanid Khaganate, whose khan Ibrahim Tamgach (1040 to 1068) built a madrasa at state expense and had a public hospital and a madrasa where medicine was also taught established.

The city’s greatest period came under Timur, who made it his capital in 1370 and over 35 years rebuilt most of it, settling in it artisans and craftsmen from across his empire. By his orders walls 8 km in circumference separated the city from its surroundings. The city then had a population of about 150,000. Ruy Gonzalez de Clavijo, the ambassador of Henry III of Castile, visited between 8 September and 20 November 1404 and recorded the building that never stopped. Ulugh Beg continued the work from 1409.
sections.rulers:
Samarkand was a Sogdian city under the Achaemenids and fell to Alexander in 329 BCE. After the Seleucids, Greco-Bactrians and Kushans, the Sasanians took it around 260 CE. The Xionites conquered it between 350 and 375 CE, it was part of the Kidarite state from 457 to 509, and the Hephthalites held it until the Gokturks, allied with the Sasanians, won it around 560.

The armies of the Umayyad Caliphate under Qutayba ibn Muslim captured the city around 712. The Abbasid commander Abu Muslim, governor of Khorasan and Transoxiana from 750 to 755, made it his residence. The Samanids ruled from 875 to 999, followed by the Karakhanids, the Seljuqs and the Khwarazmshahs. The Mongols took the city in 1220, and it remained part of the Chagatai Khanate until 1370, when Timur made it the capital of the Timurid Empire.

Nomadic Uzbek warriors took control in 1500, and in 1501 Muhammad Shaybani took the city and was crowned there, making it the capital of the new Bukhara Khanate. From 1599 to 1756 the Ashtarkhanids ruled it as part of that khanate, and from 1756 to 1868 the Manghud emirs of Bukhara. Russia annexed the city in 1868, and in 1886 it became the capital of the Samarkand Oblast of Russian Turkestan.
sections.life:
Samarkand was long a place of many faiths. Under Sasanian rule it was an important site of Manichaeism. A Nestorian chair was established in the 5th century and became a metropolitanate at the start of the 8th, and when the Umayyads captured the city most of its people were Zoroastrians, with Buddhists, Hindus, Manichaeans, Jews and Christians among them. Qutayba settled an Arab garrison in the city, razed its Zoroastrian fire temples and had a mosque built, and most of the population adopted Islam. Benjamin of Tudela reported 50,000 Jews in the city in 1170. Under the Mongols the khanate allowed Christian bishoprics, and a Roman Catholic eparchy served several thousand Catholics from 1329 to 1359.

The city also became a centre of learning. According to legend, the first paper mill of the Islamic world was founded there after the Battle of Talas in 751. Under Ulugh Beg astronomers and mathematicians gathered from across the Islamic world, among them Jamshid al-Kashi, Qadi Zada al-Rumi and Ali Qushji, and in 1428 he built an observatory whose chief instrument was a wall quadrant with a radius of 40 metres. Many classical Persian poets lived in or visited Samarkand, and Tajik, a variety of Persian, is still reported as the most common native language of the city, though no census was taken in Uzbekistan between 1989 and 2026.
sections.crises:
The Mongols took Samarkand in 1220. According to Juvayni, Genghis Khan killed all who had taken refuge in the citadel and the mosque, pillaged the city completely and conscripted 30,000 young men and 30,000 craftsmen. The conquest destroyed most of the city’s monuments, though the complex of Qutham ibn Abbas survived. Khan Baraq sacked the city again to pay an army. In 1365 a revolt against Chagatai rule, the Sarbadar uprising, centred on the Registan.

The city was largely abandoned in the early 1720s, and Nader Shah invaded the region in 1740. In 1868 a Russian force under General von Kaufman took the citadel, and the small Russian garrison of 500 men was then besieged; an assault led by Abdul Malik Tura, Baba Beg of Shahrisabz and Jura Beg of Kitab was repelled with heavy losses. An earthquake in 1897 destroyed the marble columns of the Bibi-Khanym mosque.

The Soviet period destroyed some of the city’s buildings. The madrasa of Shaybani Khan was completely destroyed, and most of the Orthodox churches built in the early 20th century were demolished. In the Second World War a number of Samarkand’s citizens were sent to Smolensk, and many were captured or killed there, while thousands of refugees from the occupied western regions of the USSR fled to the city.
sections.legacy:
The Timurid and Uzbek periods made the most important architectural contributions to the city: the Registan, whose first building was the madrasa Ulugh Beg built between 1417 and 1420, with the Sherdar and Tilakari madrasas added between 1612 and 1656; the Gur-i Amir mausoleum; the Bibi-Khanym mosque, begun by Timur after his campaign in India of 1398 and 1399, which had about 450 marble columns raised with the help of 95 elephants; and the Shah-i-Zinda necropolis, founded in the 11th century by the Qarakhanid rulers. Their cobalt and turquoise tilework is well known.

The Russian section of the city was built west of the old city after 1868, and the Trans-Caspian railway reached Samarkand in 1888. It was the capital of the Uzbek SSR from 1925 to 1930, before Tashkent replaced it. The city’s 2,500th anniversary was widely celebrated in 1970. UNESCO added Samarkand to its World Heritage List in 2001 as Samarkand, Crossroads of Cultures.

The city is today the second largest in Uzbekistan, with about 882,000 people. It is divided into an old city with the historical monuments and a new city developed under the Russian Empire and the Soviet Union. Its people include Tajiks, Uzbeks, Russians and many smaller communities, and the ethnic balance is disputed.

summary: Samarkand, in the Zarafshan valley of Uzbekistan, was a Sogdian city taken by Alexander, the Arabs, the Mongols and the Russians. Timur made it his capital in 1370, and Ulugh Beg built his observatory there. It is the second-largest city of Uzbekistan.
notes: START: the article gives no founding date ("no direct evidence"); I used c. 700 BCE (Institute of Archaeology of Samarkand) with circa true and mention the proposed 8th-7th century BCE range.

AFRASIAB: the article does not describe Afrasiab as the Sogdian city or give its history; it names Afrasiyab only as the "ancient site" where Nestorian remains were found. I wrote only that, and could not tell the Afrasiab/Sogdian story the brief asked for.

Timur's walls are given as "walls 8 km (5 mi) in circumference" and "a population of about 150,000" at this time (not dated more closely than Timur's rule); I kept that. The article gives no other population figures for any earlier period.
Paper: the article says "Legend has it", so the paper claim is attributed as legend both in dyk and in life.
Mongol sack of 1220: only Juvayni is quoted with 30,000 + 30,000; the article gives no death figure. Khan Baraq's sack has no date.

The article's History has "Samarkand was captured c. 260 AD" by the Sasanians and the Xionites 350-375 AD; Hephthalite dates not given except "until c. 560". The "Battle of Bukhara, c. 560" is as given.
The article says the Samanids ruled 875-999 and the Samanid Empire is described as the 9th century capital; I used 875-999.
Samanid, Seljuq and Khwarazmshah dates after 999 not given in detail. Western Qarakhanid capital "from 1040 to 1212".

The Soviet-era Samarkand: "Turkestan Provisional Government 1922" capital omitted for space. Samarkand as the first capital of the Uzbek SSR 1925-1930: the article says "initial capital ... from 1925 until 1930".

The tomb of Imam Bukhari and other shrines, the gardens (Yelu Chucai 1218), Marco Polo, Ibn Battuta (1333) and the literature section left out for space. The 1897 earthquake and the 1720s abandonment are as the article states them. "Nader Shah invaded in 1740": the article says "the region", not the city.

The article says the Shaybani Khan madrasa was "completely destroyed during the Soviet era" and that "most" Orthodox cathedrals and churches built in the early 20th century "were demolished while Samarkand was part of the USSR"; I attributed both to the Soviet period without naming who ordered them.

The present-day population (882,000 "as of 2026") is written without the year as the guide asks; check against your own rule. Language: the article says Tajik is "de facto the most common native language" and that official reports differ; I hedged with "reported" and "disputed".
The legacy paragraph says the 2,500th anniversary was celebrated in 1970: the article says it was widely celebrated with the support of Sharaf Rashidov; I did not name him.

The Registan: the article says the Sarbadar uprising of 1365 had the Registan as its "focal point" and that a Friday mosque was built there decades after the Mongol conquest; the Shaybani madrasa date 1504 is the first dated record.
